children.text: XView worked similarly. It had a small handful of variadic functions for its API that you passed lists of arguments into.

IMHO the main problems with this idea is that it isn't type-safe and it's wasting a lot of stack space for the tags.

> I've often wondered where it came from

Don't know but the other place where I've seen this idea is when initializing OpenGL contexts on some platforms. This involves defining attribute key/value pairs like this:

    int attributes[] =
    {
        GLX_RED_SIZE, 8,
        GLX_GREEN_SIZE, 8,
        GLX_BLUE_SIZE, 8,
        GLX_ALPHA_SIZE, 8,

        GLX_DEPTH_SIZE, 24,
        GLX_STENCIL_SIZE, 8,

        GLX_DOUBLEBUFFER, True,

        None
    };
Of course OpenGL is a bit later than AmigaOS, but not by much :)

Yes indeed. I've often wondered where it came from - did they invent it, or was it inspired by something on another platform?

(For the uninitiated, taglists are freeform lists of TAG / value pairs, which you would typically supply through varargs functions - something like OpenScreenTags(&newscreenstruct,SA_WIDTH,320,SA_HEIGHT,256,SA_DISPLAYID,myscreenmode,TAG_DONE); )

children.author: icedchai
children.text:
Yes, that was neat at the time: an array of key/value structs for extensibility. The "keys" were a #define somewhere in the header files. The original Amiga APIs (before OS 2.0) did not have tag lists and it was painful to work with.

I started learning C on an Amiga with OS 1.3, then moved to a 2.0 machine. Fun times.

I always thought Amiga's "tag list" concept was really nice. You easily could extend the API w/o breaking the ABI, which was essential for its shared library concept. And it essentially gave you named arguments too.

children.text:
Of course there is, you can do that in initializtion lists, passing fields from one field into the other.

This is a tiny example, with constructor initialization lists, which is possible since C++ARM, and I am not getting creative with what is actually possible.

https://godbolt.org/z/66TjPK49b

But the programmers must be able to foresee all possible effects of a different initialization order, supposing that it matters, otherwise they cannot write correct code.

Normally classes/structures should be defined in such a way that the order of initializing the members does not matter.

If the order of initialization matters, because there exists a really good reason to make the values of some members dependent on the values of other members (which adds superfluous information to the structure, but which might save some execution time), then I think that any programming language that allows this must enforce a unique order of initialization, i.e. the member order from the structure definition. Otherwise there would be no way to guarantee that when a constructor for a member accesses another member, that member does not contain uninitialized memory, because it has not been constructed yet.

I am not sure whether there exists a reasonable way in modern C++ to access a member of a class/structure from the constructor or destructor of another member, so unless one makes special efforts to circumvent this, e.g. by using some global variable that points to the structure whose constructors or destructors are currently executed, I think that in C++ you cannot easily define a class/structure where the order of executing the member constructors and destructors matters.

If you want for some members to depend on others, that can be easily done only in a constructor of the entire structure, where all members are visible, not in the constructors of the members.

Rice theorem enters the room.

The compiler doesn't read binary libraries, nor can foresee all possible side effects for each field constructor, or base classes.

children.author: neonz80
adrian_b
quietbritishjim
children.text: That would solve one problem, and create another one: fields get initialised in a different order depending on the caller. You have a valid point but don't pretend that there's no trade off at all.

Like I have said, a possible choice in the language specification in that whenever a set of structure members are initialized, e.g. in a function invocation, the initializations shall be done in the order from the structure definition.

This would solve your problem.

Nonetheless, I do not see why in any correct code the order of member initialization may be relevant, even when different initialization orders can produce different results, because the values of some members depend on the values of other members. If the destructor of some member accesses another member that may have already been destructed, or not, there must be a way to determine this, e.g. destructing a member should replace it with some default value for that type, e.g. a zero or a NaN or a null pointer.

Accessing other members that have already been destructed may happen also in other contexts than during the explicit initialization of the structure, so it must never lead to unpredictable behavior.

One problem with this is if one of the initializers throws an exception. The already constructed members must be destroyed. With an arbitrary initialization order the compiler will have to create different code for each order used and make sure it is this code that is called during unwinding.

This should be handled by the compiler, which shall ignore any overridden initializers and then the structure fields shall be initialized in some specified order, either the order from the definition of the structure or the initializer order.

So this is not a valid excuse for the choice made by the C++ specification.

children.author: Someone
children.text:
> the committee made arbitrary changes from what C had already laid out that made the feature worse. In particular, C++ requires that the fields appear in order

I don’t see how that’s an arbitrary change. C++ initializes members in order of the definition of a class.

Making reading order follow that IMO is the right thing to do (and yes, they didn’t do that for class initializer lists (https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/constructor: “The order of member initializers in the list is irrelevant”), but that’s widely considered a mistake (https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/dpcpp-cpp-compi..., https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/error-messages/compile...)

As is usual for C++, the committee made arbitrary changes from what C had already laid out that made the feature worse. In particular, C++ requires that the fields appear in order, which means you cannot use it to do what the linked page shows.

This isn't usually a huge deal, because C++ gives you other ways to have overloaded functions and default parameters, but it is sometimes mildly annoying.
